open_points.subject: A17 path opening of non-regular final components
open_points.text: the last component for reading with `O_NONBLOCK` as well, so a component that is no regular file is refused by the checks rather than waited on
open_points.question: Is refusal without blocking required for every non-regular Linux file type, even though `O_NONBLOCK` does not guarantee that for every device or filesystem, or is `O_NONBLOCK` only a best-effort measure?
options: Guarantee that no non-regular final component can block, using additional inspection or opening machinery
Open with `O_NONBLOCK`, then check the opened object, accepting any blocking behavior Linux documents for that object
Declare file types or filesystems for which opening can block unsupported
open_points.default_guess: Open read-only with `O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK`, check the resulting descriptor with `fstat`, and accept documented Linux device-specific behavior.

open_points.subject: A17 component-open failures
open_points.text: a component that cannot be opened so, for whatever reason, making the file one that cannot be read
open_points.question: Do transient syscall failures such as `EINTR` immediately make the file unreadable, or must the kernel retry interrupted opens and reads before refusing?
options: Refuse after the first failed syscall, including `EINTR`
Retry only interruption-class failures such as `EINTR`
Retry a broader closed set of transient failures
open_points.default_guess: Retry `EINTR` and treat every other open or read failure as unreadable.

open_points.subject: A18 exclusive data-directory lock
open_points.text: At start it takes an exclusive lock in the data directory; a second process on the same directory refuses to start.
open_points.question: What object and Linux locking primitive define this lock, when is it acquired relative to validation, and for exactly how long is it held?
options: A fixed regular lock file using `flock`, held until process exit
A fixed regular lock file using POSIX or OFD record locking, held until process exit
A lock on the data-directory descriptor or SQLite database
open_points.default_guess: Use a fixed owner-only regular lock file with a nonblocking exclusive `flock`, acquired before store inspection and held for the process lifetime.

open_points.subject: A18 data-directory pathname
open_points.text: Every file of the directory is opened without following symbolic links; a link found at start stops the start
open_points.question: Does the no-symlink rule also cover the configured data directory itself and every component leading to it, and how are absolute, relative, `.`, `..`, repeated-slash and trailing-slash paths walked?
options: Apply A17-style component-by-component no-follow traversal to the data-directory path and all descendants
Require only the final data-directory entry and entries beneath it not to be symbolic links
Allow symlinks in the path to the data directory but forbid them below its resolved root
open_points.default_guess: Apply the A17 component-by-component traversal rules to the data-directory path and use its opened descriptor as the root for all descendant access.

open_points.subject: A18 private ownership and permissions
open_points.text: The directory and everything in it are private to the kernel's user; the kernel refuses to start otherwise.
open_points.question: What exact ownership, permission-bit, ACL and hard-link conditions count as private, and are they checked only at startup or again when an entry is used after startup?
options: Require ownership by the effective kernel user and no group/other permission bits, checking at startup and on every later open
Require exact modes such as `0700` for directories and `0600` for files
Check only whether the kernel user can access the entries and rely on host administration for exclusivity
open_points.default_guess: Require the effective kernel user to own every entry with no group or other permission bits, and recheck an entry whenever it is opened.

open_points.subject: A18 allowed directory entries
open_points.text: The data directory holds one SQLite database with every kernel record, a content-addressed area of value bytes and file fixtures named by digest, and the run spool, one subdirectory per run.
open_points.question: What happens at startup or later access when the data directory contains an unexpected non-symlink entry or a non-regular object such as a FIFO, socket or device?
options: Refuse startup or the encountering store call for every unrecognised entry or wrong file type
Ignore unrecognised entries but refuse a wrong type at a required path
Permit any non-symlink type that the relevant operation can open
open_points.default_guess: Refuse unexpected entries and require regular files or directories at every defined store path.

open_points.subject: A18 startup checks and cleanup
open_points.text: At start it takes an exclusive lock in the data directory; ... the kernel refuses to start otherwise. ... a link found at start stops the start ... On start, temporary files, value bytes no record names ... and the spool directories ... are removed
open_points.question: In what order are locking, ownership and permission validation, symlink inspection, database opening, orphan cleanup and recovery performed, and which failure is reported when several are present?
options: Specify one total startup-check order and report its first failure
Group checks into phases with a first failure only within each phase
Allow implementations to report any detected startup failure
open_points.default_guess: Open and validate the directory, acquire the lock, validate all existing entries, open and validate the database, perform cleanup, then run recovery.

open_points.subject: A18 failed startup cleanup
open_points.text: On start, temporary files, value bytes no record names ... are removed; nothing else is. A spool directory that cannot be removed does not stop the start
open_points.question: Does failure to remove a temporary file or an unreferenced value byte stop startup, remain for a later startup like an unremovable spool directory, or get ignored differently?
options: Stop startup for temporary-file or unreferenced-value cleanup failure
Continue startup and retry all cleanup failures on a later start
Continue only for spool-directory failures; define separate behavior for each other category
open_points.default_guess: Continue startup, never serve the orphan, and retry its removal at a later start.

open_points.subject: A18 store order for atomic multi-record writes
open_points.text: The current activation ... is the one recorded last; the store has one writer, so records have one order. ... Every change is one call to the store module and one transaction inside it.
open_points.question: When one transaction writes several records, what is their order in the single store order, and may records share one position?
options: Every record receives a distinct consecutive global position in a specified semantic insertion order
All records from one transaction share a position and use a specified secondary order
Order is defined only within each record type
open_points.default_guess: Assign every record a distinct position from one global sequence, in the order the store call's contract lists its writes.

open_points.subject: A18 surface request serialization
open_points.text: Surface requests are handled one at a time in the order they arrive
open_points.question: Which observable event establishes arrival order for requests received concurrently: first transport byte, complete MCP message, successful decoding, or dispatcher enqueue?
options: Order by first byte received
Order by completion of the full MCP message
Order by insertion into a single dispatcher queue after framing or decoding
open_points.default_guess: Order requests by insertion into a single FIFO dispatcher queue after a complete MCP message has been framed.

open_points.subject: A18 crash-safe file and record publication
open_points.text: Value bytes and spooled files are written to a temporary file, flushed, checked against their digest and size, and then renamed into place; a completed file a record names is never overwritten
open_points.question: What does `flushed` require, must the containing directory be flushed, and what ordering between file publication and the SQLite commit guarantees that a committed record cannot name a missing file after a crash or power loss?
options: `fsync` the temporary file, rename it, `fsync` the parent directory, then commit the database with durable SQLite settings
Flush only user-space buffers before rename and rely on filesystem and SQLite defaults
Commit the database first and repair or fail records whose files are absent after restart
open_points.default_guess: Fully sync the temporary file and parent directory before committing any database record that names the published file.

open_points.subject: A18 missing or corrupted published files
open_points.text: a completed file a record names is never overwritten
open_points.question: What does startup or a later store call do if a database record names a value, fixture or spool file that is missing, has the wrong size, or no longer matches its digest?
options: Refuse startup on any missing or corrupt durable file
Start, but fail only operations that encounter the damaged file
Repair from another equal content-addressed copy when possible and otherwise refuse startup
open_points.default_guess: Refuse startup when a durable named value or fixture is missing or corrupt; derive ended-run spool expectations from run records.

open_points.subject: A20 non-Linux hosts
open_points.text: A release runs on Linux and on no other host ... Another system ... is unsupported: the kernel neither tests for it nor defines what it does there
open_points.question: Must the kernel detect a non-Linux host and refuse to start, or does `on no other host` merely define the support boundary while execution there is entirely undefined?
options: Detect the operating system and refuse startup unless it is Linux
Perform no host check; packaging and support are Linux-only and behavior elsewhere is undefined
Permit startup only when required Linux constants and calls are present, without checking the OS name
open_points.default_guess: Perform no explicit OS check and treat the release and packaging as Linux-only, because the text says the kernel does not test unsupported systems.

open_points.subject: A20 supported Linux and filesystem semantics
open_points.text: a Linux or file system on which a call these rules rely on — opening with the flags they name, locking, renaming, flushing — does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported
open_points.question: Which documented contracts and guarantees must a Linux kernel and filesystem provide to be supported, especially for the unspecified lock and flush operations of A18?
options: Name the exact syscalls, flags and durability guarantees required, with any excluded filesystem classes
Treat every Linux filesystem as supported unless a relevant call returns an explicit failure
Define support operationally by a release qualification matrix while leaving the kernel without runtime probes
open_points.default_guess: Name the exact syscalls selected by A17 and A18 and require their documented local-filesystem atomicity and durability guarantees; use no runtime filesystem allowlist.
